How Octopuses Taste the World

By Mara Lindqvist

Each sucker carries thousands of chemical receptors, which let an octopus taste whatever it touches.

An octopus exploring a reef does not need to see its dinner to know it has found it. Each sucker carries thousands of chemical receptors, which let an octopus taste whatever it touches. A single arm sweeping through a crevice gathers a running report of the rocks, shells, and animals hiding inside.

For years, researchers assumed that this information traveled straight to the brain for a decision. That turned out to be only half the story. Roughly two thirds of an octopus’s neurons sit in its arms rather than its head, and those arm neurons do a surprising amount of work on their own.

Arms that make choices

In a series of experiments, biologists offered octopuses a mix of real crabs and crab-shaped decoys. The arms consistently grabbed the real crabs and released the decoys within a fraction of a second, often before the animal’s eyes had turned toward the object. The team concluded that the arms were filtering what they touched and passing along only the promising finds.

The researchers describe this as a “taste-by-touch” system: the receptors identify a chemical signature, and the local nerve cord decides whether the object is worth holding. Only then does the central brain get involved, which frees it to keep watching for predators.

Why spread the thinking out?

An octopus has eight arms that can each bend at almost any point, which creates far more possible movements than a brain could plan one by one. Letting each arm handle routine choices is a way of coping with that complexity. Engineers who build soft robots have taken note, because their machines face the same problem of controlling a body with no fixed joints.

There is a cost, though. Because the arms act partly on their own, an octopus sometimes has to rein them in. Observers have watched arms keep probing a crevice after the animal had clearly decided to move on, as if the arm had not yet received the message.

What it means for us

The octopus is a reminder that intelligence does not have to live in one central place. Its body solves problems in parallel, with the brain acting more like a manager than a dictator. Studying that arrangement may help scientists design robots that adapt to messy, unpredictable environments, and it challenges the old assumption that a bigger brain is the only route to clever behavior.
